questions.question: What are the core Azure services a Java backend developer should know — App Service, AKS, and Azure Functions?
questions.title: Azure Core Services for Java Backend Developers
questions.direct_answer: Java backend developers on Azure primarily work with App Service for managed web apps, AKS for container orchestration, and Azure Functions for serverless compute. Each targets a different operational model and team maturity level.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands Azure's compute tiers and can choose the right service for the workload.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating all three services as interchangeable or defaulting to AKS for everything without considering operational overhead.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Azure Container Apps as a middle ground between App Service and AKS, and discuss cold-start trade-offs for Functions.

sections.title: The Real Question Is What You're Trading, Not What You're Picking
sections.content:
Every Java backend eventually runs somewhere, and the real interview question isn't whether you can name App Service, AKS, and Functions — it's whether you understand what you trade when picking one. The axis is **operational ownership versus control**.

At one end sits Azure Functions: you deploy a single method, Azure handles the runtime, scaling, and process lifecycle. Your team writes zero infrastructure code. At the other end is AKS — a full Kubernetes cluster where you own node pools, networking, ingress controllers, service meshes, and every YAML manifest. App Service occupies the middle ground: deploy a JAR or WAR, Azure manages the OS and patches, but you choose the SKU, configure autoscale rules, and manage deployment slots.

The gap most candidates miss is **Azure Container Apps**, which runs containers on a managed Kubernetes substrate with KEDA-based autoscaling and Dapr integration — but without Kubernetes manifests. For teams that need more than App Service but can't justify the operational cost of AKS, Container Apps is often the right answer.

Cold starts are another blind spot. Functions on the Consumption plan incur 2–15 seconds of Java startup latency, which makes them unsuitable for synchronous API endpoints with tight SLOs. The Premium plan with pre-warmed instances solves this, but at that point you're paying for always-on compute — which erodes the cost advantage of serverless.

sections.title: Four Services on One Spectrum — What You Deploy vs. What You Manage
sections.content:
Each service makes a different trade on what you control and what Azure manages. The table below maps the dimensions that actually affect your architecture decisions, not just feature checkboxes.

| Dimension | App Service | Azure Functions | Container Apps | AKS |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| You deploy | JAR/WAR or container | Annotated method class | Container image | Container + K8s manifests |
| Scaling | Rule-based (CPU, HTTP queue) | Event-driven, scale-to-zero | KEDA-based, scale-to-zero | HPA + cluster autoscaler |
| Cold start | None (always running) | 2–15s on Consumption plan | Sub-second with min replicas | None (pods always running) |
| Networking | VNet integration available | VNet requires Premium plan | Built-in VNet integration | Full CNI control |
| You manage | Scaling rules, deployment slots | Function code only | Container image, env vars | Nodes, networking, all manifests |
| Best fit | Single app, predictable traffic | Event handlers, scheduled jobs | Microservices without K8s ops | Complex multi-service platforms |
| Baseline cost | ~$70 (B1) to ~$280 (P1v3)/mo | Free tier + per-execution | ~$50 min + consumption | ~$290+ (3-node cluster)/mo |

The cost column matters more than most candidates realize. A single Spring Boot API on App Service P1v3 costs roughly $140/month. The same service on a minimal 3-node AKS cluster costs $290+ before adding monitoring, ingress controllers, and operational tooling.

sections.title: Matching Workload Shape to the Right Service
sections.content:
**Start with App Service** when the team has one to three Spring Boot services with predictable traffic. You get deployment slots for blue-green releases, built-in autoscale, Java 17/21 runtime support, and managed TLS — all without container expertise. A P1v3 plan with 2 vCPUs and 8 GB RAM handles most intermediate workloads at roughly $140/month.

**Graduate to Container Apps** when you need scale-to-zero behavior, multiple cooperating microservices, or Dapr sidecars for service invocation and pub/sub. Container Apps uses KEDA scaling rules, so a Service Bus queue trigger can scale replicas from zero to fifty based on queue depth — something App Service autoscale cannot express. The trade-off is that you must containerize your application, but you never touch Kubernetes primitives.

**Choose AKS** only when you need capabilities that require direct cluster access: custom operators, Istio or Linkerd service mesh, StatefulSets for stateful workloads, multi-tenant node pool isolation with taints and tolerations, or integration with an existing platform team's Kubernetes toolchain. The operational cost is real — node image upgrades, certificate rotation, CNI troubleshooting, and etcd backup management are ongoing responsibilities.

**Use Functions** for event-driven glue: a blob trigger that generates thumbnails, a timer that purges expired sessions, a Service Bus trigger that dispatches notifications. These are tasks that run briefly, infrequently, and independently. Forcing a full Spring Boot context into a Function adds 10+ seconds of cold start with no benefit.

sections.title: The AKS Default and the Container Apps Blind Spot
sections.content:
The most common mistake in interviews is **defaulting to AKS because Kubernetes appears on every job description**. A single Spring Boot API serving 200 requests per second does not need a Kubernetes cluster. The operational overhead — node upgrades every six weeks, CNI plugin compatibility, PodDisruptionBudget tuning, RBAC for developer access — outweighs any orchestration benefit for simple workloads. Interviewers specifically test whether you can articulate *when not to use AKS*.

The second trap is ignoring Container Apps entirely. It launched in GA in 2023 and directly addresses the segment between App Service and AKS. Mentioning it signals that you follow Azure's evolving compute landscape rather than reciting a 2020-era service catalog. The combination of KEDA scaling, Dapr integration, and revision-based traffic splitting covers most microservice needs without a single line of Kubernetes YAML.

A strong answer walks the interviewer through a decision tree: start with App Service, evaluate Container Apps when you need event-driven scaling or multi-service orchestration, and reserve AKS for teams with dedicated platform engineering capacity. This shows you think about operational cost alongside technical capability.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **App Service for managed PaaS; AKS for full Kubernetes; Container Apps for serverless containers** — choose based on required operational control; App Service is the simplest starting point for Spring Boot
- **Azure SQL for relational workloads** — managed PostgreSQL or SQL Server; JDBC and Hibernate work without modification; built-in HA with failover replicas across Availability Zones
- **Cosmos DB for global distribution and NoSQL** — multi-region active-active; tunable consistency from Strong to Eventual; Spring Data Cosmos provides repository-style access
- **Service Bus for enterprise messaging; Event Hub for high-throughput streaming** — Service Bus for transactional queues with dead-letter and sessions; Event Hub for Kafka-compatible event ingestion at millions of events per second
- **Azure Container Registry (ACR) for Docker images** — private registry in the same region as AKS or Container Apps; integrated authentication via Azure AD; eliminates DockerHub rate limiting

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Azure compute for Java backend services forms a spectrum based on how much operational ownership you want — from fully managed PaaS to raw VMs. Knowing where each service sits on that spectrum makes the right choice obvious.

**Compute — from most managed to least**
- Azure App Service is the highest-level managed hosting — deploy a JAR or Docker image, configure the runtime, and Azure handles the OS, patching, TLS, and auto-scaling; the right choice for most Spring Boot services where you don't need Kubernetes features
- AKS (Azure Kubernetes Service) gives you a managed Kubernetes control plane while you manage the worker node pools — the right choice when you need pod autoscaling, custom resource definitions, sidecar patterns, or multi-container workloads
- Azure Container Apps is the middle ground — managed Kubernetes-based infrastructure with simplified configuration; deploy containers without writing Kubernetes YAML; auto-scales to zero for cost efficiency on variable workloads

**Data storage**
- Azure SQL Database is managed PostgreSQL/SQL Server with built-in HA, geo-redundancy, and elastic scaling — full JDBC and Hibernate support with no code changes
- Cosmos DB is a globally distributed NoSQL database with multiple consistency models and APIs (SQL, MongoDB, Cassandra); use when you need sub-10ms global reads or a multi-region active-active setup

**Messaging and integration**
- Azure Service Bus is the enterprise messaging backbone — queues for point-to-point, topics for pub/sub fan-out, with dead-letter queues, sessions, and deferred processing
- Azure Event Hub is a high-throughput event streaming platform — similar to Kafka, with consumer group semantics and partition-based parallelism; use for telemetry ingestion and event streaming at scale

questions.question: How do you deploy a Spring Boot application to Azure Spring Apps?
questions.title: Deploying Spring Boot to Azure Spring Apps
questions.direct_answer: You deploy to Azure Spring Apps using the Azure CLI or Maven plugin: provision the service instance, create an app, then deploy the JAR. Azure manages the Spring runtime, service discovery, and config server.

interviewer_intent.testing: Hands-on familiarity with Azure Spring Apps provisioning and deployment workflow.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing Azure Spring Apps with a generic App Service deployment — missing the spring-specific config server and service registry features.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the managed Spring Cloud Config Server, eureka service registry, and blue-green deployment via staging deployments.

sections.title: Why a Spring-Specific PaaS Exists When App Service Already Deploys JARs
sections.content:
Deploying a Spring Boot application to a generic cloud VM or App Service means you're responsible for service discovery, configuration management, and health routing — the entire Spring Cloud infrastructure that your microservices depend on. Azure Spring Apps exists because Microsoft and VMware recognized that teams shouldn't have to operate their own Eureka cluster, Config Server, and Spring Cloud Gateway just to run a few Spring Boot services.

The platform provisions a **managed Eureka service registry** and a **managed Spring Cloud Config Server** backed by a Git repository. Your Spring Boot services register with Eureka automatically on startup and pull externalized configuration from the Config Server — without deploying or maintaining either component. This is the critical distinction from a generic App Service deployment, and the mistake most candidates make is treating Azure Spring Apps as just another PaaS for JARs. The Spring-specific managed components are the entire point.

Azure Spring Apps also provides **staging deployments** for blue-green releases. You deploy a new version to the staging slot, validate it against the staging endpoint, and swap traffic with a single CLI command. If the new version fails, you swap back — the previous production deployment is still running.

sections.title: Three Commands From Nothing to a Running Service
sections.content:
The deployment workflow has three commands: create the service instance, create an app within it, and deploy the JAR. The service instance is the container for all your apps and their shared managed infrastructure. Each app within the service maps to one deployable Spring Boot artifact.

```bash
az group create --name my-rg --location eastus

az spring create \
  --name my-spring-service \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --sku Standard

az spring app create \
  --service my-spring-service \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --name order-api \
  --runtime-version Java_17 \
  --assign-endpoint true

az spring app deploy \
  --service my-spring-service \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --name order-api \
  --artifact-path target/order-api-1.0.jar
```

The `--assign-endpoint true` flag creates a public URL for the app. In production, you'd typically leave this off and route traffic through Azure Application Gateway or Front Door instead. The `--sku Standard` tier includes the managed Config Server and Eureka — the Basic tier omits these, which removes the primary advantage of the platform.

sections.title: The Managed Spring Cloud Features That Justify the Platform
sections.content:
The managed Config Server connects to a Git repository you specify, and every app in the service instance pulls configuration from it at startup. This implements the Spring Cloud Config pattern without deploying `spring-cloud-config-server` as a separate service.

```bash
az spring config-server set \
  --service my-spring-service \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --config-file config-server-settings.json
```

The configuration file points to a Git repo with `application.yml` profiles organized by service name and environment. When your Spring Boot app starts, it resolves `spring.config.import=configserver:` automatically — the platform injects the Config Server URI. The managed Eureka registry allows your services to discover each other by application name without hardcoded URLs.

The **Enterprise tier** adds commercial VMware Tanzu components: Application Accelerator for project scaffolding, API Portal for centralized API documentation, and Application Live View for real-time actuator inspection across all deployed apps. For most teams, the Standard tier covers the essential Spring Cloud infrastructure. The Enterprise tier becomes relevant when operating dozens of services with a dedicated platform team managing the shared infrastructure.

sections.title: Zero-Downtime Releases Through Staging Deployments
sections.content:
Staging deployments are how you achieve zero-downtime releases without building your own blue-green infrastructure. Rather than deploying directly to production, you create a staging deployment, validate it, and swap.

```bash
az spring app deployment create \
  --service my-spring-service \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --app order-api \
  --name green \
  --artifact-path target/order-api-2.0.jar

curl https://my-spring-service-order-api-green.azuremicroservices.io/actuator/health

az spring app set-deployment \
  --service my-spring-service \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --name order-api \
  --deployment green
```

The first command deploys the new version as a named deployment (`green`) alongside the existing production deployment. The staging deployment gets its own URL for smoke testing. The `set-deployment` command swaps production traffic to the green deployment atomically. If something goes wrong, running `set-deployment` again with the original deployment name rolls back instantly — both deployments remain running until you explicitly delete one.

Your CI/CD pipeline should create the staging deployment, run integration tests against the staging URL, and only swap if tests pass. The swap itself is a metadata change at the platform level — no pods restart, no connections drop.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Managed Config Server and Eureka eliminate self-hosted Spring Cloud infrastructure** — Azure Spring Apps provisions these from a Git repo and service registry URL; no pods to manage, patch, or scale
- **Deploy with CLI or Maven plugin** — `az spring app deploy --artifact-path target/app.jar` deploys the JAR; `mvn azure-spring-apps:deploy` integrates with the Maven build pipeline
- **Environment variables override `application.properties`** — configure database URLs and feature flags in the portal or CLI; reference secrets via `spring-cloud-azure-starter-keyvault-secrets` to avoid plaintext in config
- **Application Insights auto-collects metrics and traces** — attach the Java agent or use the built-in integration; HTTP latency, exception rates, and dependency traces appear without SDK changes
- **Horizontal scaling with Availability Zone distribution** — `az spring app scale --instance-count N`; Azure distributes across AZs automatically; configure health checks so instances are replaced if they fail

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Azure Spring Apps (formerly Azure Spring Cloud) is a managed platform specifically designed for Spring Boot services — it provides built-in Spring Cloud infrastructure like Config Server and Service Registry without you running and maintaining those components.

**What Azure Spring Apps manages for you**
- Spring Cloud Config Server: Azure Spring Apps provisions and manages Config Server backed by a Git repository — which means your Spring Boot services pull configuration from a central Git repo without you deploying a Config Server pod
- Eureka Service Registry: Spring Boot services register and discover each other through a managed Eureka instance; you configure your application.properties with the registry URL and Azure handles the rest
- Distributed tracing: built-in Application Insights integration collects traces from every service without manual SDK configuration

**Deploying a Spring Boot application**
- Package the Spring Boot app as a JAR; deploy with the Azure CLI: `az spring app deploy --name my-service --artifact-path target/app.jar`; or use the Azure Spring Apps Maven plugin: `mvn azure-spring-apps:deploy`
- Configure environment variables and connection strings in the Azure portal or CLI — these override `application.properties` values; keep database URLs and passwords in Azure Key Vault, referenced via the Spring Cloud Azure Key Vault starter

**Scaling and monitoring**
- Azure Spring Apps scales horizontally by setting the instance count per service — `az spring app scale --name my-service --instance-count 5`; it distributes instances across Availability Zones automatically
- Application Insights is the default monitoring integration — it collects HTTP request metrics, latency distributions, dependency traces, and exceptions without any SDK changes in your application

Use Azure Spring Apps when: you're already committed to Spring Cloud patterns, want managed Config Server and Eureka, and don't need custom Kubernetes capabilities. Use AKS when you need full Kubernetes control.

questions.question: When should a Java developer choose Azure Service Bus over Azure Event Hubs for messaging?
questions.title: Azure Service Bus vs Event Hubs — Messaging Choice for Java
questions.direct_answer: Use Service Bus for enterprise messaging patterns (queues, topics, dead-letter, sessions, at-most-once/at-least-once delivery). Use Event Hubs for high-throughput event streaming where you need replay and consumer groups — analogous to Kafka.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of messaging semantics — queues vs. streams, delivery guarantees, and when each model fits.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Choosing Event Hubs for all messaging because it sounds more modern, missing that it lacks dead-letter queues and per-message TTL.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Event Hubs Kafka surface — you can point a Kafka producer/consumer at Event Hubs without code changes.

sections.title: Does the Consumer Destroy the Message or Observe the Event?
sections.content:
The decision between Service Bus and Event Hubs comes down to one question: **does the consumer destroy the message, or does it observe the event?** Service Bus is a message broker — once a consumer acknowledges a message, it's gone from the queue. Event Hubs is a partitioned event log — consumers read events at their own offset, and the events remain in the log for days. These are fundamentally different messaging models, and picking the wrong one creates architectural problems that are expensive to fix later.

Service Bus supports enterprise messaging patterns that Event Hubs deliberately omits: dead-letter queues for failed messages, per-message TTL, duplicate detection windows, and sessions for ordered processing by partition key. When a payment processing pipeline needs to guarantee that a failed charge is inspected by an operator rather than silently dropped, Service Bus's dead-letter queue is the mechanism. Event Hubs has no equivalent — failed events require application-level error handling and a separate error topic.

The common mistake is choosing Event Hubs for all messaging because it handles higher throughput and sounds more modern. A payment command queue processing 50 messages per second needs Service Bus's delivery guarantees far more than it needs Event Hubs' million-event-per-second capacity. Conversely, a clickstream ingestion pipeline feeding analytics, audit, and ML consumers simultaneously needs Event Hubs' fan-out model — Service Bus subscriptions can't replay consumed messages.

sections.title: Broker vs Log — Where the Semantics Diverge
sections.content:
The table below highlights the capabilities that drive architectural decisions. These aren't feature checkboxes — each missing capability in Event Hubs forces you to build an alternative in application code.

| Capability | Azure Service Bus | Azure Event Hubs |
|---|---|---|
| Core model | Message broker (queue / pub-sub) | Partitioned event log (stream) |
| After consumption | Message deleted from queue | Event retained for configured window |
| Throughput | Thousands of operations/sec | Millions of events/sec |
| Dead-letter queue | Built-in, automatic on failure | Not available |
| Message replay | Not possible (consumed once) | Replay from any offset in retention |
| Per-message TTL | Configurable per message | Retention is partition-level only |
| Duplicate detection | Built-in time window | Not built-in |
| Ordered processing | Sessions (FIFO per session key) | Per-partition ordering only |
| Consumer model | Competing consumers (one wins) | Consumer groups (all read independently) |
| Kafka compatibility | Not available | Kafka wire protocol supported |
| Spring starter | `spring-cloud-azure-starter-servicebus` | `spring-cloud-azure-starter-eventhubs` |

sections.title: Command-Style Work vs Observation-Style Streaming
sections.content:
**Service Bus fits command-style messaging.** When a message represents work that must be processed exactly once — place an order, charge a card, send a notification — Service Bus guarantees that one consumer handles it. If processing fails after the maximum delivery count, the message moves to the dead-letter queue rather than being lost. Sessions enforce ordered processing per partition key, so all messages for `order-123` are processed sequentially even with multiple competing consumers.

The Spring integration uses `@ServiceBusListener` with automatic message completion on success and dead-letter on repeated failure. Your handler method focuses on business logic; the framework handles acknowledgment.

**Event Hubs fits observation-style streaming.** When multiple independent systems need to react to the same event — an analytics pipeline, an audit log, and a recommendation engine all observing user activity — Event Hubs lets each consumer group read the entire stream at its own pace. Replay is built in: if the analytics pipeline had a bug last Tuesday, you can reprocess from that offset without republishing events.

The **Kafka-compatible endpoint** is Event Hubs' underrated feature. You configure a standard Kafka producer with the Event Hubs namespace as the bootstrap server, and your existing Kafka client code works without modification. Authentication uses SASL/PLAIN with the Event Hubs connection string. This is a practical migration path for teams moving from self-managed Kafka to Azure without rewriting producer and consumer code.

sections.title: What Event Hubs Doesn't Have Will Surprise You
sections.content:
**Event Hubs lacks enterprise messaging primitives** that many developers assume are standard. There is no dead-letter queue — if your consumer throws an exception, you must handle the failure in application code by retrying, logging, or forwarding to an error topic. There is no per-message TTL — retention applies to the entire partition, not individual events. There is no built-in duplicate detection — idempotent processing is your responsibility.

Teams that choose Event Hubs for command-style workloads end up rebuilding these features in application code: a custom dead-letter topic, manual deduplication with a seen-ID cache, and TTL checks in the consumer. That's significant engineering effort to recreate what Service Bus provides out of the box.

The architecture that works best in practice often uses both services together. Event Hubs ingests high-volume events — clickstreams, telemetry, audit logs. A stream processor (Azure Stream Analytics or a Spring Cloud Stream consumer) enriches and filters those events, then publishes the resulting commands to Service Bus for reliable downstream processing. This gives you the throughput and fan-out of Event Hubs for observation, combined with the delivery guarantees of Service Bus for action.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Service Bus: each message delivered to one consumer; Event Hub: each consumer group reads the full stream** — Service Bus for transactional point-to-point or topic fan-out; Event Hub for parallel consumption of the same event stream by independent consumers
- **Service Bus dead-letter queue captures unprocessable messages** — messages that fail processing N times (or exceed TTL) move to the DLQ; inspect and replay from the DLQ without affecting the main queue
- **Event Hub retains events for replay** — default 1-7 days; consumers control their own offset; a new consumer group can replay from the beginning; Service Bus messages are deleted after `complete()`
- **Event Hub supports Kafka protocol** — `bootstrap.servers` points to the Event Hub namespace; existing Kafka clients connect without code changes; managed Kafka without cluster operations
- **Service Bus sessions for ordered per-entity processing** — a session ID groups related messages; a single consumer processes all messages for one session in order; essential for order state machines and workflow orchestration

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Azure Service Bus and Event Hub both move messages between services, but they serve fundamentally different consumption models — Service Bus is a message broker for transactional workloads; Event Hub is an event stream for high-throughput ingestion.

**Service Bus — transactional message broker**
- Service Bus delivers a message to exactly one consumer from a queue — when the consumer reads a message and calls `complete()`, it's removed; if the consumer fails and calls `abandon()` or the lock expires, it becomes visible again for reprocessing
- Topics and subscriptions extend this with fan-out: one message published to a topic can be delivered to multiple subscriptions, each with its own filter and dead-letter queue
- Service Bus supports message sessions (ordered processing per entity), deferred messages, scheduled delivery, and dead-letter queues for unprocessable messages — which makes it the right choice for order processing, payment workflows, and any use case where each message must be processed exactly once with retry

**Event Hub — high-throughput event stream**
- Event Hub stores events in partitioned ordered logs — multiple consumer groups can independently read the same stream from different offsets, which means one stream of telemetry events can be consumed independently by a metrics aggregator, a real-time dashboard, and a cold storage archiver
- Events are retained for a configurable period (1-7 days by default, up to 90 days with Event Hub Premium) — which means consumers can replay events without the producer knowing or caring
- Event Hub supports Kafka protocol — existing Kafka producers and consumers can connect to Event Hub with only a connection string change, which makes it a managed Kafka alternative on Azure

**Spring integration**

questions.question: How do you integrate Azure Key Vault with a Spring Boot application for secrets management?
questions.title: Azure Key Vault Integration with Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: Add the spring-cloud-azure-starter-keyvault-secrets dependency, configure the Key Vault URI in application.properties, and grant the app a Managed Identity with Key Vault Secrets User role. Secrets are then accessible as Spring properties.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to eliminate plaintext secrets from application config using cloud-native secret management.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Hard-coding the Key Vault client secret or connection string instead of using Managed Identity for passwordless access.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain how Spring Cloud Azure maps Key Vault secret names to Spring property names, and mention secret rotation without restart.

sections.title: The Credential Leak Problem That Key Vault Actually Solves
sections.content:
Every Spring Boot application has secrets — database passwords, API keys, encryption certificates — and the default approach of putting them in `application.yml` or environment variables creates a security problem that grows with the team. Anyone with access to the Git repository or deployment configuration can read every credential. Azure Key Vault solves this by moving secrets into a managed vault with access control, audit logging, and automatic rotation — but the integration has to be seamless or developers will work around it.

Spring Cloud Azure's Key Vault property source makes secrets appear as ordinary Spring `Environment` properties. You reference `${db-password}` in `@Value` or `@ConfigurationProperties` exactly as you would with any configuration value. The library fetches secrets from Key Vault at startup and caches them, so your business code has zero awareness that a vault exists.

The critical security practice — and the mistake most candidates make — is authentication. The wrong approach is creating a service principal with a client secret and storing that secret in `application.yml`. You've just moved the secret-storage problem from one file to another. The right approach is **Managed Identity**: Azure assigns your App Service, AKS pod, or Function an identity automatically, and `DefaultAzureCredential` acquires a token from the instance metadata endpoint without any credential in your configuration.

sections.title: One Dependency, One Property, No Credentials in Config
sections.content:
The setup requires one dependency and one configuration property. The `spring-cloud-azure-starter-keyvault-secrets` starter registers a `PropertySource` that resolves against your Key Vault during application startup.

```xml
<dependencyManagement>
  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>com.azure.spring</groupId>
      <artifactId>spring-cloud-azure-dependencies</artifactId>
      <version>5.19.0</version>
      <type>pom</type>
      <scope>import</scope>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

<dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>com.azure.spring</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-cloud-azure-starter-keyvault-secrets</artifactId>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>
```

The only required configuration is the vault endpoint. No credentials appear in the file — `DefaultAzureCredential` handles authentication automatically.

```yaml
spring:
  cloud:
    azure:
      keyvault:
        secret:
          endpoint: https://my-vault.vault.azure.net/
```

With this in place, any secret stored in the vault becomes available as a Spring property. A Key Vault secret named `db-password` is resolved when you inject `@Value("${db-password}")`. The library loads all secrets at startup by default, which means the number of secrets in your vault affects startup time — a vault with 500 secrets adds noticeable latency.

sections.title: Why Managed Identity Makes Client Secrets Obsolete
sections.content:
Managed Identity eliminates credential management entirely. When your application runs on App Service, Functions, or AKS, Azure provides a token endpoint on the instance metadata service. `DefaultAzureCredential` calls this endpoint to acquire an Azure AD token scoped to Key Vault — no username, no password, no client secret.

```bash
az webapp identity assign --name my-app --resource-group my-rg

az role assignment create \
  --role "Key Vault Secrets User" \
  --assignee $(az webapp identity show --name my-app \
    --resource-group my-rg --query principalId -o tsv) \
  --scope /subscriptions/<sub>/resourceGroups/my-rg/providers/Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/my-vault
```

The RBAC role assignment is required even after enabling the identity — authentication and authorization are separate. `Key Vault Secrets User` grants read-only access to secrets. For applications that also write or rotate secrets, `Key Vault Secrets Officer` is the appropriate role.

Locally, `DefaultAzureCredential` falls back to your `az login` session. In CI/CD, it reads from environment variables (`AZURE_CLIENT_ID`, `AZURE_TENANT_ID`, `AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET`). The same Spring Boot code works across all environments without configuration changes — only the credential source differs.

sections.title: Hyphen-to-Dot Translation and Rotation Without Restarts
sections.content:
Key Vault secret names use hyphens (`db-password`), but Spring property names typically use dots or camel case. The Spring Cloud Azure library translates hyphens to dots automatically, so `db-password` in the vault resolves as `db.password` in Spring's `Environment`. If your property is `spring.datasource.password`, name the Key Vault secret `spring-datasource-password`.

For secret rotation without application restart, configure a refresh interval that periodically re-reads secrets from the vault.

```yaml
spring:
  cloud:
    azure:
      keyvault:
        secret:
          property-sources:
            - endpoint: https://my-vault.vault.azure.net/
              refresh-interval: 30m
```

The library refreshes the property source every 30 minutes, picking up rotated secrets. However, beans that were initialized with the old secret value won't automatically update — a `DataSource` created with the old password keeps using it until the connection pool cycles. For database credentials, combine this with `spring.datasource.hikari.max-lifetime=1800000` (30 minutes) so connections are replaced after the secret refreshes.

Key Vault throttles at **4,000 transactions per 10 seconds per vault**. If your application has many services hitting the same vault at startup, stagger startup times or use separate vaults per team. Store non-secret configuration — feature flags, connection strings without credentials — in Azure App Configuration instead, which has much higher throughput limits.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Spring Cloud Azure Key Vault starter = secrets as Spring properties** — `spring.cloud.azure.keyvault.secret.endpoint` configured; `@Value("${db-password}")` resolves from Key Vault at startup; no SDK calls in business code
- **Managed Identity eliminates credential management** — App Service, AKS, and Container Apps get an Azure AD identity automatically; `DefaultAzureCredential` uses it; no client ID or secret in application.properties
- **`DefaultAzureCredential` works both locally and in production** — falls back to Azure CLI credential locally; Managed Identity in Azure; same code path, no environment-specific credential configuration
- **Secrets are cached at startup by default** — rotation doesn't take effect until restart; configure `refresh-interval` for configuration values; use rolling restarts for credential rotation
- **Never store Key Vault client secrets in code or config files** — use Managed Identity instead; a client secret in `application.properties` defeats the purpose of using Key Vault

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Azure Key Vault integration with Spring Boot works through a Spring `PropertySource` — secrets stored in Key Vault appear as regular Spring properties, which means your `@Value("${db-password}")` resolves from Key Vault at startup without any code changes.

**Setup**
- Add `spring-cloud-azure-starter-keyvault-secrets` to dependencies; configure `spring.cloud.azure.keyvault.secret.endpoint` with the Key Vault URI; Spring Cloud Azure auto-configures the `KeyVaultEnvironmentPostProcessor` that fetches all secrets at startup
- Key Vault secrets are named with dashes — `db-password` — and Spring Cloud Azure maps them to properties with dots: `db.password`; configure the property-source name prefix to avoid conflicts

**Authentication — Managed Identity**
- For applications running on Azure (App Service, AKS, Container Apps), use Managed Identity — the platform provides the Azure AD identity; Spring Cloud Azure's `DefaultAzureCredential` picks it up automatically; no client secrets in config
- For local development, use `az login` — `DefaultAzureCredential` falls back to the Azure CLI credential when running outside Azure; the same code works locally and in production

**Runtime secret refresh**
- By default, Spring Cloud Azure loads secrets at startup and caches them for the process lifetime — which means a secret rotation in Key Vault doesn't take effect until the application restarts
- Configure `spring.cloud.azure.keyvault.secret.property-sources[0].refresh-interval` for periodic re-fetch — appropriate for non-sensitive config; for security credentials, prefer a rolling restart strategy after rotation

**Certificate management**
- Key Vault also stores certificates and keys; use Key Vault-integrated TLS for App Service so Azure rotates and deploys certificates automatically — which means your app never has expired TLS certificates due to manual rotation failures

questions.title: Azure Blob Storage with Spring Boot (azure-storage-blob)
questions.direct_answer: Use the Spring Cloud Azure starter for Blob Storage. Inject BlobServiceClient or BlobContainerClient, and call upload/download methods. Authenticate with Managed Identity — no connection strings in code.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical knowledge of Azure storage SDK integration in Spring Boot, including authentication and streaming uploads.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using a storage account connection string instead of Managed Identity or SAS tokens, or loading the full blob into memory for large files.

sections.title: The OutOfMemoryError Waiting Inside Every Naive File Upload
sections.content:
File handling in a Spring Boot application sounds simple until you upload a 2 GB video and the server runs out of heap memory. The default approach — `MultipartFile.getBytes()` — loads the entire file into the JVM heap before sending it to storage. For large files, this causes `OutOfMemoryError` or, worse, forces you to over-provision heap to handle peak file sizes. Azure Blob Storage solves the storage side; the integration challenge is keeping the data path streaming end-to-end.

Spring Cloud Azure auto-configures `BlobServiceClient` and `BlobContainerClient` beans based on your `application.yml`. Authentication follows the same `DefaultAzureCredential` pattern as Key Vault — Managed Identity in Azure, `az login` locally. The configuration requires only the storage account name; no connection string or account key appears in your files.

The second pattern most candidates miss is **SAS token delegation**. Instead of proxying every file download through your Spring Boot server — which consumes bandwidth and thread pool capacity — you generate a time-limited Shared Access Signature URL and redirect the client directly to Blob Storage. The blob serves the file; your server just issues the signed URL.

sections.title: One Starter, One Property, Managed Identity for Auth
sections.content:
The dependency and configuration mirror the Key Vault pattern: one starter, one property, Managed Identity for authentication.

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>com.azure.spring</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-cloud-azure-starter-storage-blob</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

```yaml
spring:
  cloud:
    azure:
      storage:
        blob:
          account-name: mystorageaccount
```

Grant the application's Managed Identity the `Storage Blob Data Contributor` role on the storage account. This role allows read, write, and delete operations on blobs. For read-only workloads, use `Storage Blob Data Reader` instead — least privilege matters.

```bash
az role assignment create \
  --role "Storage Blob Data Contributor" \
  --assignee <managed-identity-principal-id> \
  --scope /subscriptions/<sub>/resourceGroups/my-rg/providers/Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/mystorageaccount
```

With this setup, Spring auto-configures a `BlobServiceClient` bean that you can inject into any service. The client handles connection pooling, retry policies, and authentication token refresh automatically.

sections.title: Streaming End-to-End — Never Buffer the Full File
SAS Tokens — Let Azure Serve the File, Not Your Server
Key Points
sections.content:
- **SAS URL for direct client upload avoids server bottleneck** — server generates a time-limited signed URL; client uploads directly to blob storage; server never handles the bytes; eliminates bandwidth and memory cost for large uploads
- **`BlobServiceClient` from Spring Cloud Azure starter** — auto-configured with `spring.cloud.azure.storage.blob.account-name`; Managed Identity provides authentication; no storage account key in configuration
- **`BlobClient.upload(inputStream, length)` for server-side uploads** — stream-based upload avoids loading large files into memory; set `Content-Type` and `Content-Disposition` for correct browser download behavior
- **Lifecycle management for cost optimization** — configure policies to transition from Hot to Cool after 30 days, to Archive after 90 days; blob storage costs 10x less in Archive tier than Hot
- **Soft delete recovers accidental overwrites** — enable with a 7-30 day retention window; blobs deleted or overwritten can be restored within the window; critical for user-generated content

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Azure Blob Storage integration with Spring Boot follows the same architectural decision as S3: proxy the bytes through your server, or generate a SAS URL and let the client upload directly.

**Spring Cloud Azure setup**
- Add `spring-cloud-azure-starter-storage-blob`; configure `spring.cloud.azure.storage.blob.account-name`; inject `BlobServiceClient` or the higher-level `StorageResource` as a Spring `Resource` — which means Spring's resource abstraction works with blob URLs using the `azure-blob://` prefix

**SAS (Shared Access Signature) URLs — for direct client upload**
- Generate a SAS URL on the server: `BlobServiceClient.generateAccountSas()` or `BlobClient.generateSas()` with a `BlobSasPermission` and expiry — the client receives a time-limited URL to upload directly to blob storage without passing bytes through your server
- Which means your server avoids the bandwidth and memory cost of large file uploads; blob storage receives the data directly from the client

**Direct upload via server**
- When you need to validate, virus-scan, or transform content before storage: `blobClient.upload(inputStream, length, true)` streams the data to blob storage; set `Content-Type` and `Content-Disposition` on the upload to ensure correct browser download behavior
- For large files, use `BlobClient.uploadFromFile()` or block blob upload with parallel transfers: `ParallelTransferOptions` configures block size and max concurrency

**Access tiers**
- Hot tier for frequently accessed data; Cool tier for data accessed infrequently (lower storage cost, higher access cost); Archive tier for data retained for compliance that's rarely accessed — lifecycle management policies transition blobs automatically between tiers based on last-modified date
- Enable soft delete on the container so accidental overwrites or deletions can be recovered within the retention window

questions.question: How do you choose between Azure SQL Database and Azure Cosmos DB for a Java application?
questions.title: Azure SQL Database vs Cosmos DB for Java Apps
questions.direct_answer: Use Azure SQL Database for relational, transactional workloads where data consistency and SQL semantics matter. Use Cosmos DB for globally distributed, schema-flexible, high-throughput scenarios where eventual consistency is acceptable.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of trade-offs between relational and NoSQL databases in a cloud context, not just API differences.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Choosing Cosmos DB for its global distribution without factoring in Request Unit (RU) pricing complexity or the consistency level trade-offs.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Cosmos DB's five consistency levels, the Spring Data Cosmos integration, and partition key design impact on performance and cost.

sections.title: A Data Modeling Decision That's Expensive to Reverse
sections.content:
The choice between Azure SQL Database and Cosmos DB is not a feature comparison — it's a data modeling decision that's expensive to reverse. **Azure SQL gives you joins, constraints, and multi-table ACID transactions at the cost of single-region write locality. Cosmos DB gives you global active-active writes with sub-10ms latency at the cost of careful partition key design and a fundamentally different consistency model.**

Most candidates can recite that SQL is relational and Cosmos is NoSQL. What separates strong answers is understanding the second-order consequences. Azure SQL with JPA/Hibernate means your team writes standard JPQL queries, uses `@Transactional` for business logic spanning multiple tables, and benefits from decades of relational optimization tooling. Cosmos DB with Spring Data means your team designs access patterns around a partition key upfront, writes repository methods that always include the partition key, and chooses from five consistency levels — each with measurable latency and cost trade-offs.

The common mistake is choosing Cosmos DB for global distribution without understanding **Request Unit pricing** or partition key design. A poorly chosen partition key creates a hot partition that throttles writes regardless of how many RUs you've provisioned. And RU costs are opaque — a cross-partition query that scans 100 partitions can consume 50x more RUs than the same query restricted to one partition.

sections.title: Relational Predictability vs Global Reach — The Dimensions That Matter
sections.content:
The table below focuses on the dimensions that drive real architectural decisions rather than API-level differences. Pay particular attention to the transaction scope and pricing model — these create the most surprises in production.

| Dimension | Azure SQL Database | Azure Cosmos DB |
|---|---|---|
| Data model | Relational (tables, joins, foreign keys) | Document, key-value, graph, column |
| Transactions | Full ACID across tables | ACID within a single partition key only |
| Global writes | Read replicas only (active-passive) | Active-active multi-region writes |
| Consistency | Strong (serializable) always | Five levels: Strong → Eventual |
| Schema | Fixed, requires migrations | Schema-flexible per document |
| Scaling | Vertical (vCores/DTUs) | Horizontal (partition + RU/s) |
| Spring integration | Spring Data JPA + Hibernate | Spring Data Azure Cosmos (custom repos) |
| Query language | Full T-SQL with joins | SQL-like API (no cross-document joins) |
| Pricing | Compute + storage, predictable | RU/s provisioned or serverless, variable |
| Latency (single region) | 5–15ms typical | < 10ms guaranteed at p99 |

sections.title: Relational Domains Stay Relational, Access-Pattern Domains Go Cosmos
sections.content:
**Choose Azure SQL Database** when your domain has natural relational structure. Order management with orders, line items, products, and customers connected by foreign keys is the canonical example. JPA's ability to traverse these relationships with lazy loading, cascading operations, and JPQL joins means you model the domain naturally. Multi-table transactions are essential — deducting inventory and recording the order line must succeed or fail together.

Azure SQL also fits when your team has deep Hibernate expertise. The migration from on-premises SQL Server to Azure SQL Database is near-zero friction — same T-SQL dialect, same JDBC driver, same Hibernate mappings.

**Choose Cosmos DB** when data access patterns are partition-key-centric and global distribution matters. A user profile store accessed by `userId`, a product catalog queried by `categoryId`, or IoT telemetry partitioned by `deviceId` — each has a clear partition key with high cardinality. Cosmos DB's five consistency levels let you tune the trade-off per operation: use **Session consistency** for read-your-own-writes (the default and most common choice), **Bounded Staleness** for cross-region reads that lag by at most *k* versions or *t* seconds, or **Eventual** for maximum throughput on non-critical reads.

The partition key design is the single most important technical decision. A key with low cardinality — like `status` with values `active`/`inactive` — creates a hot partition that bottlenecks throughput. The ideal key distributes reads and writes evenly: `userId`, `orderId`, or `tenantId`.

sections.title: RU Pricing and the Missing JPA — Two Traps That Catch Teams Late
sections.content:
**Request Unit pricing catches teams by surprise.** Every Cosmos DB operation consumes RUs proportional to the document size, index complexity, and query scope. A point read by partition key and ID costs approximately 1 RU. A cross-partition query scanning 50 partitions can cost 200+ RUs for the same result set. If you provision 400 RU/s (the minimum) and a query consumes 80 RUs, five concurrent requests exhaust your budget and trigger 429 throttling.

The practical consequence is that **Cosmos DB requires upfront access pattern design**, not the ad-hoc querying that SQL databases support. Every query should include the partition key. Reports and analytics that scan across partitions belong in a separate system — use Change Feed to replicate data to Azure Synapse or Azure SQL for analytical queries.

Another trap: **Cosmos DB's Spring Data integration does not support JPA**. The `@Repository` interface looks similar, but there's no lazy loading, no entity relationships, no JPQL. Each document is a self-contained JSON object, and you query with SQL-like syntax against the document structure. Teams expecting to reuse their JPA entity model will need a complete data access layer rewrite. This isn't a limitation of the Spring library — it's fundamental to how document databases work.

**Choosing between them**

questions.question: How does Azure Active Directory authentication work with Spring Security?
questions.title: Azure Active Directory Authentication with Spring Security
questions.direct_answer: Use the spring-cloud-azure-starter-active-directory dependency to configure OAuth2/OIDC authentication. Azure AD acts as the authorization server, issuing JWT tokens that Spring Security validates via the JWKS endpoint.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of OAuth2/OIDC flow in the context of Azure AD and how Spring Security integrates with external identity providers.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Manually parsing JWT tokens in filters instead of using Spring Security's built-in resource server support with Azure AD's JWKS endpoint.

sections.title: Why Writing Your Own JWT Filter Is the Wrong Starting Point
sections.content:
Most candidates who integrate Azure AD with Spring Security start by writing a custom filter that extracts the JWT bearer token, Base64-decodes it, validates the signature, and checks the claims manually. This is exactly the wrong approach. Spring Security's `oauth2-resource-server` module already does all of this — it fetches Azure AD's signing keys from the JWKS endpoint, validates the token signature, checks expiration and audience, and creates a `SecurityContext` with the token's claims. The Spring Cloud Azure starter layers additional convenience on top: it auto-configures the issuer URI, maps Azure AD app roles to Spring authorities, and handles the JWKS key rotation that breaks manual implementations.

The authentication flow starts outside your application. A client obtains a JWT access token from Azure AD's `/token` endpoint. Your Spring Boot service receives this token in the `Authorization: Bearer` header and validates it against Azure AD's public signing keys — never by calling Azure AD on every request. The keys are cached and refreshed periodically, so token validation is a local cryptographic operation with no network round-trip.

What makes Azure AD integration deeper than generic OAuth2 is the authorization model. Azure AD supports **app roles** — custom roles defined in your application's manifest and assigned to users or groups by an admin. These roles appear in the JWT's `roles` claim and map to Spring Security authorities with an `APPROLE_` prefix, enabling `@PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('APPROLE_Admin')")` without any custom role-mapping code.

sections.title: What Happens Between the Bearer Token and the SecurityContext
sections.content:
When a request arrives with a bearer token, Spring Security's `BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter` extracts the token and passes it to a `JwtDecoder`. The decoder performs four operations: it verifies the token's cryptographic signature against Azure AD's JWKS keys (cached from `https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenant}/discovery/v2.0/keys`), checks that the token hasn't expired, validates the `iss` (issuer) claim matches your tenant, and confirms the `aud` (audience) claim matches your application's client ID.

The audience validation is critical for security. The `aud` claim prevents **token confusion attacks** — if you have two APIs registered in Azure AD, a token issued for API-A should be rejected by API-B even though both trust the same Azure AD tenant. Without audience validation, an attacker who obtains a token for any application in the tenant could access your API.

```yaml
spring:
  cloud:
    azure:
      active-directory:
        enabled: true
        credential:
          client-id: ${AZURE_CLIENT_ID}
        profile:
          tenant-id: ${AZURE_TENANT_ID}
```

The Spring Cloud Azure starter configures all of this from three properties. The `client-id` becomes the expected audience, the `tenant-id` determines the issuer URI, and the library discovers the JWKS endpoint automatically from Azure AD's OpenID Connect metadata.

sections.title: App Roles vs Groups — Scoped Permissions Beat Tenant-Wide Memberships
On-Behalf-Of Flow — Preserving User Identity Across Service Chains
sections.content:
In a microservice architecture, Service A receives a user request and needs to call Service B on behalf of that user. The **On-Behalf-Of (OBO) flow** allows Service A to exchange the user's incoming token for a new token scoped to Service B, preserving the user's identity through the service chain.

This matters for audit trails. If Service A used its own client credentials to call Service B, the downstream audit log would show 'Service A accessed this resource' — losing the information about which user initiated the request. With OBO, the downstream token still identifies the original user, so every service in the chain can log the real caller's identity.

The OBO flow requires Service A to have a client secret or certificate and API permissions granted between the two applications. In Spring, the `azure-spring-boot-starter-active-directory` supports this through the `AadOboOAuth2AuthorizedClientProvider`, which handles the token exchange automatically when you use `WebClient` with the appropriate OAuth2 configuration.

**Conditional Access policies** add another layer at the identity platform level. Azure AD can enforce MFA, device compliance, or IP-based restrictions at token issuance. These policies apply before your Spring Security configuration is even evaluated, so you get enterprise-grade access controls without implementing them in each service. A single Conditional Access rule requiring MFA for all API access protects every Spring Boot service that trusts the tenant — no per-service code changes needed.

sections.content:
- **Spring Cloud Azure AAD starter auto-configures OAuth2 and JWT validation** — add the dependency and client-id/tenant-id config; Spring Security handles token validation, role extraction, and `@PreAuthorize` enforcement
- **`application-type=web-api` for API-only services** — configures Bearer token validation instead of OAuth2 login redirect flow; appropriate for REST APIs called by other services or SPAs
- **Roles in JWT `roles` claim drive `@PreAuthorize`** — assign App Roles in Azure AD portal; Spring Security maps them to Spring's `GrantedAuthority`; use `hasRole('Admin')` in annotations
- **Managed Identity for service-to-service calls** — calling service uses `DefaultAzureCredential` to acquire a token for the target; no client secrets; Azure AD acts as the credential broker
- **Validate `tid` claim in multi-tenant apps** — a multi-tenant App Registration accepts tokens from any Azure AD tenant; validate the tenant ID claim against an allowlist to prevent unauthorized tenant access

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Azure Active Directory (Azure AD, now Entra ID) integration with Spring Security works through standard OAuth2 and OIDC protocols — which means your Spring Boot service participates in the Azure identity ecosystem using the same OAuth2 support built into Spring Security.

**How it works**
- Register your Spring Boot application in Azure AD as an App Registration; Azure AD acts as the OAuth2 authorization server and OIDC identity provider
- Add `spring-cloud-azure-starter-active-directory`; configure `spring.cloud.azure.active-directory.credential.client-id`, `tenant-id`, and `client-secret`; Spring Security auto-configures an OAuth2 login flow and JWT validation for Bearer tokens

**Token validation for API-only services**
- For REST APIs that accept Bearer tokens (no browser login): configure `spring.cloud.azure.active-directory.application-type=web-api`; the starter configures Spring Security to validate incoming JWT tokens from Azure AD
- The JWT contains the user's roles and claims — use `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ROLE_Admin')")` on controller methods; Spring Security extracts roles from the `roles` claim in the Azure AD JWT automatically

**Service-to-service authentication with Managed Identity**
- For a Spring Boot service calling another Azure service or a downstream API: use Managed Identity with the Azure Identity SDK; `DefaultAzureCredential` acquires a token for the target resource without credentials in code
- Register both services as App Registrations; grant the calling service's Managed Identity the appropriate Application Role on the target service's App Registration

**Multi-tenant configuration**
- A multi-tenant app registration accepts tokens from any Azure AD tenant — configure `spring.cloud.azure.active-directory.profile.tenant-id=common`; validate the `tid` claim in the token to restrict which tenants are allowed

sections.title: Four Handoffs, Four Places to Leak Credentials or Break Deployments
sections.content:
Getting a Java application from a Git commit to a running Kubernetes pod involves four handoffs: build the application, package it as a container image, push the image to a registry, and update the Kubernetes cluster to run the new image. Each handoff is a place where teams introduce security vulnerabilities or operational fragility. The most common mistake is storing Azure Container Registry credentials as plaintext secrets in the pipeline — a practice that creates rotation overhead and a credential leak surface.

Azure's solution is the **ACR-AKS integration**: a single CLI command (`az aks update --attach-acr`) grants the AKS cluster's kubelet identity the `AcrPull` role on your registry. After this, AKS pulls images from ACR without `imagePullSecrets` in your pod specs. No registry passwords in Kubernetes secrets, no rotation schedules, no credential expiration alerts.

The second critical practice is **immutable image tags**. Tagging every image with the Git commit SHA (not `latest`) ensures that every deployment is traceable to a specific commit, rollbacks deploy a known-good image, and image vulnerability scans are attributable to a specific build. A tag of `latest` is ambiguous — it could be yesterday's build or last month's, and `kubectl rollout undo` might pull a completely different image than expected.

sections.title: ACR-AKS Integration — No Registry Passwords in Your Cluster
sections.content:
The setup is two commands: create the registry and attach it to your cluster. Under the hood, this creates an RBAC role assignment that grants the kubelet's Managed Identity pull access.

```bash
az acr create \
  --name myregistry \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --sku Standard

az aks update \
  --name my-cluster \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --attach-acr myregistry
```

The `--attach-acr` command grants the AKS cluster's kubelet managed identity the `AcrPull` role on the registry. The kubelet uses this identity to authenticate image pulls without any Kubernetes secret. This works regardless of whether ACR and AKS are in the same subscription — cross-subscription role assignments are supported.

For the CI pipeline's push access, use a service principal with the `AcrPush` role or — better — federated credentials with GitHub Actions OIDC. The `azure/login` GitHub Action supports OIDC-based authentication, eliminating long-lived credentials from your pipeline secrets entirely. This means no stored passwords anywhere in the system: AKS pulls with Managed Identity, and the pipeline pushes with OIDC-federated tokens.

sections.title: Multi-Stage Dockerfile — 800 MB Build Image to 180 MB Runtime
sections.content:
A multi-stage Dockerfile separates the build environment from the runtime, dramatically reducing the final image size and attack surface.

```dockerfile
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY pom.xml .
RUN mvn dependency:go-offline -B
COPY src ./src
RUN mvn package -DskipTests -B

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/target/*.jar app.jar
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
```

The build stage uses a full Maven image with the JDK (~800 MB), but the final image uses only the JRE on Alpine Linux (~180 MB). The `dependency:go-offline` step is cached by Docker layer caching — dependencies only re-download when `pom.xml` changes, not on every code change. This reduces build times from minutes to seconds for iterative development.

The Alpine-based JRE image also has a smaller CVE surface. Enable **Defender for Containers** on your ACR to scan every pushed image for known vulnerabilities. Configure it to block deployments of images with critical CVEs by using an Azure Policy assignment that denies pods referencing images with scan failures.

sections.title: The Pipeline Ties It Together — Fail Fast on Broken Deployments
sections.content:
The pipeline ties build, push, and deploy together. The critical details are tagging images with the Git commit SHA and using `kubectl rollout status` to make the pipeline fail if the deployment doesn't succeed.

```yaml
name: Deploy to AKS
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: azure/login@v2
        with:
          client-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_CLIENT_ID }}
          tenant-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_TENANT_ID }}
          subscription-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID }}
      - run: |
          az acr login --name myregistry
          IMAGE=myregistry.azurecr.io/my-api:${{ github.sha }}
          docker build -t $IMAGE .
          docker push $IMAGE
      - uses: azure/aks-set-context@v3
        with:
          resource-group: my-rg
          cluster-name: my-cluster
      - run: |
          kubectl set image deployment/my-api \
            my-api=myregistry.azurecr.io/my-api:${{ github.sha }}
          kubectl rollout status deployment/my-api --timeout=300s
```

The `kubectl rollout status --timeout=300s` command blocks until the rollout succeeds or fails. Without it, the pipeline reports success immediately after updating the image reference — even if the new pods crash-loop. The Kubernetes Deployment should specify `maxUnavailable: 0` in the rolling update strategy and point the readiness probe at `/actuator/health/readiness` with `initialDelaySeconds: 15` to give the JVM time to start. If the new image fails readiness checks, the rollout stalls and the pipeline fails — catching the broken deployment before users are affected.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Git SHA as image tag enables traceability and rollback** — `myacr.azurecr.io/my-service:abc1234` links every deployed image to a commit; rollback is `kubectl set image` with an older SHA
- **ACR in the same region as AKS eliminates cross-region transfer** — AKS pulls images from ACR over the Azure backbone; no public internet bandwidth cost; image pulls are fast even for large JVM images
- **`az aks update --attach-acr` configures pull permissions** — grants the AKS Managed Identity `acrPull` on ACR; no imagePullSecrets in Kubernetes manifests; credentials managed by Azure AD
- **Helm tracks release history** — `helm upgrade` records the previous release; `helm rollback my-service 1` reverts to the previous version's manifests and image tag in one command
- **AKS rolling deployment by default** — `strategy: RollingUpdate` with `maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0` ensures old pods stay until new pods pass readiness checks; configure readiness probe on `/actuator/health/readiness`

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The Azure container deployment pipeline — build, push to ACR, deploy to AKS — follows a consistent four-stage pattern regardless of whether you use Azure DevOps Pipelines, GitHub Actions, or Jenkins.

**Build stage**
- Build the Spring Boot JAR with Maven or Gradle, then build the Docker image — a multi-stage Dockerfile builds the JAR in a JDK stage and copies the artifact to a JRE final image to minimize image size
- Use the Git commit SHA as the image tag: `docker build -t myacr.azurecr.io/my-service:$(git rev-parse --short HEAD) .` — which means every deployed image is traceable to a specific commit, making rollback straightforward

**Push to ACR**
- Authenticate to ACR with `az acr login --name myacr` (development) or a service principal with `acrPush` role (CI); push the tagged image
- ACR geo-replication mirrors images to the same regions as AKS clusters — which means image pulls from AKS are fast and don't traverse the public internet; use ACR in the same region as AKS to avoid cross-region latency

**Deploy to AKS**
- Update the Kubernetes Deployment manifest with the new image tag: `kubectl set image deployment/my-service my-service=myacr.azurecr.io/my-service:SHA`
- Or use Helm: update the `image.tag` value and `helm upgrade my-service ./charts/my-service --set image.tag=SHA`; Helm tracks release history, making `helm rollback` a single command

**AKS authentication to ACR**
- Attach ACR to AKS with `az aks update --attach-acr myacr` — this grants the AKS kubelet's Managed Identity the `acrPull` role on ACR; pods pull images without imagePullSecrets or stored credentials

sections.title: When a Request Takes 12 Seconds, You Need to Know Where the Time Went
sections.content:
When a user reports that an API call took 12 seconds, you need to know where that time was spent — was it the database query, the downstream HTTP call, or the garbage collector? Without an APM tool, the answer requires correlating timestamps across application logs, database slow query logs, and infrastructure metrics. Azure Application Insights solves this with distributed tracing that stitches every operation — HTTP request, JDBC query, outbound HTTP call, message processing — into a single trace.

The critical decision for Java developers is *how* to instrument. The old approach was embedding the Application Insights SDK into your code with manual `telemetryClient.trackEvent()` and `trackDependency()` calls scattered across services. The modern approach is the **Java agent** (`applicationinsights-agent.jar`), which uses bytecode instrumentation to auto-instrument the entire Spring Boot stack without touching your source code. The agent hooks into JDBC drivers, HTTP client libraries, Spring MVC, messaging frameworks, and more — all through a single JVM argument.

The agent is built on OpenTelemetry internally, which means it propagates the W3C `traceparent` header across services. When Service A calls Service B, both operations appear in the same distributed trace in the Azure portal. It also injects the trace ID into SLF4J's MDC, so every log line includes the trace and span ID — making log-to-trace correlation trivial.

sections.title: One JVM Argument, Zero Code Changes, Full Stack Coverage
sections.content:
The setup requires downloading the agent JAR and adding a JVM argument. No Maven dependencies, no code changes to your application.

```dockerfile
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY applicationinsights-agent.jar .
COPY target/app.jar .
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-javaagent:applicationinsights-agent.jar", "-jar", "app.jar"]
```

The agent reads its configuration from `applicationinsights.json` in the same directory or classpath root.

```json
{
  "connectionString": "InstrumentationKey=...",
  "role": { "name": "order-api" },
  "sampling": { "percentage": 10 }
}
```

The `role.name` identifies this service in multi-service traces — the Application Map in the Azure portal uses this name to draw the service dependency graph. The `connectionString` comes from the Application Insights resource. Sampling percentage controls what fraction of telemetry is collected.

For custom business metrics, use **Micrometer** — Spring Boot's default metrics facade. The agent exports Micrometer metrics automatically through its bridge, so `Counter`, `Timer`, and `Gauge` beans flow into Azure Monitor without additional configuration or exporter setup.

sections.title: Distributed Traces and Log Correlation — One ID Across Every Service
sections.content:
The agent propagates W3C `traceparent` headers on all outbound HTTP calls. When `order-api` calls `inventory-api`, both services' spans share the same trace ID and appear in a single end-to-end transaction view in the Azure portal.

Log correlation is equally powerful. The agent injects `trace_id` and `span_id` into SLF4J's MDC context. If your log pattern includes `%X{trace_id}`, every log line is tagged with the distributed trace ID.

```xml
<pattern>%d{HH:mm:ss} [%thread] [trace=%X{trace_id} span=%X{span_id}] %-5level %logger{36} - %msg%n</pattern>
```

This means you can take a trace ID from the Azure portal's transaction view, search for it in Log Analytics, and find every log line from every service that participated in that request. During incident investigation, this eliminates the 'which service logged what?' question entirely.

Application Insights also captures unhandled exceptions with the full stack trace, dependency durations, and request/response metadata. The **Application Map** visualizes service dependencies with health indicators — if `order-api` calls `payment-api` and payment-api's average response time degrades, the map highlights that edge in red. This gives on-call engineers a 30-second overview of system health that would otherwise require checking multiple dashboards.

sections.title: 100% Sampling at High Traffic Can Cost Hundreds Per Month
sections.content:
**Uncontrolled telemetry ingestion is the most expensive mistake** with Application Insights. At 100% sampling and 10,000 requests per second, a single service can generate over $500/month in ingestion costs. The agent's default adaptive sampling dynamically reduces volume during traffic spikes while preserving full traces for errors, slow requests, and dependency failures.

Set a **daily cap** in the Azure portal as a safety net — once the cap is reached, Application Insights stops ingesting new telemetry but continues processing alerts on existing data. Configure fixed sampling at 10% for high-traffic services (capturing every 10th request end-to-end) and leave error traces at 100% — failed requests should always be fully captured.

For actionable alerting, define rules based on SLO thresholds rather than absolute values. Alert when p99 latency exceeds 2 seconds for 5 consecutive minutes, or when error rate exceeds 1% over a 10-minute window. Azure Monitor's **smart detection** adapts to your traffic patterns and flags anomalies without manual threshold configuration — but it supplements, not replaces, explicit SLO-based alerts.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Java agent instruments without code changes** — `-javaagent:applicationinsights-agent.jar` auto-collects HTTP metrics, SQL queries, outbound calls, and exceptions; no SDK imports in business code
- **`APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING` is the only required config** — contains instrumentation key and regional endpoint; set as environment variable; agent picks it up automatically
- **Distributed trace correlation across services** — agent propagates trace IDs through HTTP headers; a slow request can be traced from API gateway through each microservice to the database query
- **Micrometer metrics auto-collected by the agent** — custom `Counter`, `Timer`, and `Gauge` metrics appear in Application Insights as custom metrics without any Insights SDK calls
- **KQL for querying telemetry** — `requests | where success == false | summarize count() by bin(timestamp, 1h)` queries error rates by hour; create alerts directly from KQL results in the portal

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Application Insights provides distributed tracing, metrics, and log aggregation for Spring Boot services on Azure — the recommended approach is the Java agent, not the SDK, because the agent instruments the application without any code changes.

**Java agent — zero-code instrumentation**
- Attach the agent as a JVM argument: `-javaagent:/path/to/applicationinsights-agent.jar`; in App Service, set `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS=-javaagent:/path/applicationinsights-agent.jar` in the application settings
- The agent auto-instruments HTTP requests (request duration, status codes), Spring Data queries (SQL timing, query text), outbound HTTP calls, and exception logging — all without any application code changes
- Application Insights collects this telemetry and correlates it with a distributed trace ID, which means a slow API call can be traced through the Spring Boot service to the database query that caused it

**Connection string configuration**
- Configure `APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING` as an environment variable or application setting — this is the only configuration the agent needs; the connection string includes the instrumentation key and the regional endpoint

**Custom telemetry with Micrometer**
- The Application Insights Java agent integrates with Micrometer automatically — custom `Counter`, `Timer`, and `Gauge` metrics registered with the `MeterRegistry` are published to Application Insights as custom metrics
- Use `TelemetryClient` from the Application Insights SDK for custom events and properties: `telemetryClient.trackEvent("OrderPlaced", properties, metrics)` adds domain events to the telemetry stream

**Querying with Kusto (KQL)**
- Application Insights stores telemetry in Log Analytics; queries use Kusto Query Language: `requests | where duration > 500 | summarize count() by bin(timestamp, 5m)` finds slow requests per 5-minute window
- Create dashboards and alerts directly in Application Insights from KQL queries
